intro: Each of us has habits of thinking that developed from our experiences, our relationships, and the world around us. This page looks at ten common patterns of belief, such as mistrust, perfectionism, and fear of rejection, and at the false beliefs that often go with them. Further down, it also lists false beliefs that often go with depression, anxiety, trauma, abuse, and substance use. It is an educational resource, not a test. Recognizing a belief in yourself does not mean something is wrong with you, and it is not a way to label others. These patterns are based on the work of Aaron Beck and other cognitive therapists, written here in plain language. Beliefs overlap, and each person’s story, culture, and faith matter. Our purpose is to notice beliefs that may be inaccurate or too rigid, question them thoughtfully, and replace them with more truthful and constructive ways of thinking.
aside: Use these examples for learning and reflection, not to label yourself or others or replace professional assessment. A preference is not inherently faulty; the target is an inaccurate generalization or rigid rule. Shared religious beliefs are not, by themselves, a sign that something is wrong.

footer: Sources: DSM-5-TR (categories); Beck, Davis, & Freeman (Eds.), Cognitive Therapy of Personality Disorders (3rd ed., 2015), and Beck Institute personality-belief materials (themes). These examples are not a validated assessment or a ranked top-five list. Schizotypal examples are educational syntheses, not an original PBQ scale. OCPD is distinct from OCD. The Common Struggles examples are plain-language educational syntheses of widely taught cognitive themes: a harsh view of oneself, one’s life, and the future; overestimated danger and underestimated ability to cope; trauma-related beliefs about safety, trust, self-blame, and the future; survivor beliefs after abuse; and permission-giving or relief-seeking beliefs about substance use. They are not a diagnosis, a treatment plan, or a validated scale.

groups.name: Mistrusting Others
beliefs: I can't let my guard down
Friendliness usually hides an ulterior motive.
I need to hide the real me in order to not get hurt.
People always try to hide what they are doing
Little things often have great significance

groups.name: Avoiding Others
beliefs: Getting close to people will cost me my freedom.
I don’t need anyone. I am better off alone.
Depending on anyone only leads to trouble.
My feelings aren’t worth sharing. Talking about them changes nothing.
Relationships take more than they give, so they aren’t worth the effort.

groups.name: Social Isolation
beliefs: What other people think of me doesn’t matter.
I’ve given up on letting people in.
Close relationships aren’t important to me.
Nothing is much fun anyway, so I might as well be on my own.

groups.name: Unusual Thinking and Social Unease
beliefs: I am fundamentally unlike other people.
My thoughts can cause unrelated events.
Unusual sensations confirm my unusual explanations.
Other people’s intentions are usually threatening.

groups.name: Rule Breaking
beliefs: Using other people is necessary to get by.
What I want matters more than other people’s rights.
Bending the truth is fine when it helps me.
Staying in control keeps me from being controlled.
If I’ve been wronged, I have the right to get even.

groups.name: Intense Emotions and Fear of Abandonment
beliefs: The people I love will eventually leave me.
If people really knew me, they would not accept me.
I can’t manage life without someone to lean on.
My feelings are so strong they will completely overwhelm me.
Any disagreement means the people I love are about to reject me.

groups.name: Need for Attention and Approval
beliefs: I must entertain people to retain affection.
Stronger displays are necessary to be heard.
My feelings reliably establish what is true.

groups.name: Specialness and Need for Admiration
beliefs: I am entitled to exceptional treatment.
Ordinary limits should not apply to me.
Other people should prioritize my needs.

groups.name: Fear of Rejection and Inadequacy
beliefs: Avoiding people and new challenges is safer than risking embarrassment.
I am inadequate and less than other people.
I am awkward and unlikable, and I have little to offer.
I must be sure people will like me before I let them know me.
Ridicule or criticism would prove I am worthless, and I could not bear it.

groups.name: Need for Care and Reassurance
beliefs: I lack the ability to cope independently.
Other people’s judgment is better than mine.
Disagreement threatens the support I need.
Keeping support requires surrendering my preferences.

groups.name: Perfectionism and Control
beliefs: My standards should govern everyone’s behavior.

sections.heading: Common Struggles — Associated Beliefs
sections.hint: Choose a box to show ten beliefs. Click again to close it.

groups.name: Depression
beliefs: There’s no use trying. I’ll only fail again.
I’m no good. I never have been.

groups.name: Anxiety
beliefs: Something terrible is about to happen.
If I feel anxious, that means I am in real danger.
I can’t cope if the worst happens.
I have to stay on guard, or I will miss the danger.
Not knowing what will happen means something is wrong.
If I don’t worry, I won’t be prepared.
These feelings in my body mean I’m about to lose control.
If people see me anxious, I won’t be able to handle it.
One small problem will turn into a disaster.
I can’t relax until I am sure everything is safe.

groups.name: PTSD
beliefs: Nowhere is really safe. Danger is about to happen again.
I can’t trust anyone. If I let my guard down, I’ll be hurt again.
What happened was my fault. I should have seen it coming and stopped it.
I’m permanently damaged by what happened, and I will never be myself again.
My future holds only more pain. I will never feel safe or whole again.
I have no control. If it happened once, nothing I do can stop it from happening again.
Other people can see that I am different now, and they will keep their distance.
When my body reacts, the danger is happening now. I am not safe even here.
If I talk about it, I will fall apart, so I have to keep it locked inside.
If I care about someone, they will be hurt, or I will lose them.

groups.name: Abuse
beliefs: What was done to me was my fault. I must have caused it.
I’m damaged and ashamed, as if what was done to me made me worthless.
If I tell someone, they won’t believe me, or they will blame me.
I don’t deserve to be safe or treated kindly.
I have to keep this secret. Speaking up would only make everything worse.
I should have fought harder or left sooner. Because I didn’t, I must have agreed to it.
Kindness is a trap. If someone is gentle with me, they are getting ready to hurt me.
I have to keep them calm. If they get angry, it is my job to fix it.
I don’t get to decide what happens to my body. Saying no doesn’t count.
Other people had it worse, so what was done to me doesn’t really count.

groups.name: Substance Abuse
beliefs: I can control it. I can stop whenever I want.
I need it to get through the day. I can’t cope without it.
I’ve earned it. After what I’ve been through, I deserve the relief.
One more time won’t matter. I’ll quit tomorrow.
This is the only thing that makes me feel okay, and nothing else will work.
A little doesn’t count. I can keep it small and still be in control.
Other people are the reason I use. If they treated me better, I wouldn’t need it.
I don’t hurt anybody else, so this is my choice and it is fine.
I’ve already messed things up, so there is no point in stopping now.
I can’t be myself around people unless I use first.
